parts.label: (a)(i)
key_concepts: mole concept in ideal gas equation
hints: Hint 1: Think about what $n$ is counting in $pV = nRT$ - it is not mass or number of molecules directly, but the chemist's way of counting a very large number of particles.
parts.proper_answer: The symbol $n$ is the amount of substance (number of moles) of gas.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link R to moles**
You are told $R$ is the molar gas constant, meaning it is defined per mole. So $n$ must be the quantity measured in moles to keep the units consistent. In physics this is called the amount of substance.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Remember the gas laws only work if temperature is measured from absolute zero, so think about which temperature scale starts at absolute zero.
parts.proper_answer: The symbol $T$ is the thermodynamic (absolute) temperature measured in kelvin.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why Celsius cannot be used**
Pressure is proportional to temperature only if zero means zero kinetic energy. That zero is absolute zero, $-273.15^{\circ}\text{C}$. So $T$ must be on the Kelvin scale, also called thermodynamic or absolute temperature.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Start by listing $p$, $V$ and $T$ in SI base units - pay special attention to converting $\text{cm}^3$ to $\text{m}^3$ and $^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $\text{K}$.
Hint 2: Think about which form of the ideal gas law links directly to number of molecules $N$ - you can use $pV = nRT$ then $N = nN_A$, or use $pV = NkT$ in one step.
Hint 3: Rearrange first to make $n$ or $N$ the subject, then substitute values to show the result is about $2.3 \times 10^{23}$.
parts.proper_answer: $V = 2.4 \times 10^3 \text{ cm}^3 = 2.4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3$, $T = 373 \text{ K}$. From $pV = nRT$, $n = pV/RT = 0.38 \text{ mol}$. $N = nN_A = 0.38 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 2.3 \times 10^{23}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Convert to SI units**
Ideal gas equations need $V$ in $\text{m}^3$ and $T$ in $\text{K}$. Since $1 \text{ m} = 100 \text{ cm}$, then $1 \text{ m}^3 = 10^6 \text{ cm}^3$. So $$V = 2.4 \times 10^3 \times 10^{-6} = 2.4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3$$ And for temperature: $$T = 100 + 273 = 373 \text{ K}$$ A common slip is to leave $T$ in Celsius or $V$ in $\text{cm}^3$.

Step 2: **Find moles from pV = nRT**
The gas obeys: $$pV = nRT$$ Rearranged: $$n = \frac{pV}{RT}$$ Substitute $p = 4.9 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}$, $R = 8.31 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1}$: $$n = \frac{4.9 \times 10^5 \times 2.4 \times 10^{-3}}{8.31 \times 373} \approx 0.38 \text{ mol}$$

Step 3: **Convert moles to molecules**
One mole contains $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}$ molecules, so: $$N = n N_A = 0.38 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{23}$$ This matches the value to be shown. Alternatively you can do it in one step with $pV = NkT$ where $k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \text{ J K}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Imagine the whole container volume is shared equally between all $2.3 \times 10^{23}$ molecules - how would you find the small volume available to just one molecule?
Hint 2: Picture each molecule sitting at the centre of its own little cube, with the cubes filling the container - how is the side length of that cube related to its volume?
Hint 3: Keep the volume in $\text{cm}^3$ since the answer is asked for in $\text{cm}$, then take the cube root of the volume per molecule to get a length.
parts.proper_answer: Volume per molecule $= V/N = 2.4 \times 10^3 / 2.3 \times 10^{23} \approx 1.0 \times 10^{-20} \text{ cm}^3$. Mean spacing $\approx (V/N)^{1/3} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-7} \text{ cm}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the volume for one molecule**
If $N$ molecules fill volume $V$, each one on average occupies: $$V_1 = \frac{V}{N}$$ Using $V = 2.4 \times 10^3 \text{ cm}^3$ and $N = 2.3 \times 10^{23}$: $$V_1 = \frac{2.4 \times 10^3}{2.3 \times 10^{23}} \approx 1.04 \times 10^{-20} \text{ cm}^3$$ Keeping $V$ in $\text{cm}^3$ saves converting back later.

Step 2: **Model spacing as a cube**
A simple but good estimate is to imagine each molecule in its own cube of side $d$. Then $d^3 = V_1$, so the mean centre-to-centre distance is: $$d = V_1^{1/3}$$ This assumes the molecules are evenly spread and ignores their actual size, which is fine for an estimate.

Step 3: **Take the cube root**
$$d = (1.04 \times 10^{-20})^{1/3} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-7} \text{ cm}$$ That is about $2 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$, many times larger than a molecule itself, which fits the ideal gas idea that molecules are far apart compared to their size.
